mainTopic: Splitting money in doubt (סומכוס) and oaths in buyer-and-seller disputes over a newborn or over which item was sold.
overview: This amud starts with a משנה about buyer-and-seller disputes when the facts are unclear. If a cow or a שפחה gives birth around the time of a sale and each side claims the baby, they split it. With two slaves or two fields, one big and one small: whoever is sure beats the one who says 'I don't know'. If both are sure and disagree, the seller swears. If neither knows, they divide. The גמרא asks why the baby is split instead of going to whoever holds it. שמואל answers that it stands in a marsh or alley, and the גמרא adds that the משנה follows סומכוס, who splits money in doubt. רבה בר רב הונא and רבא then argue whether סומכוס splits even when both sides are sure, and the גמרא tests each view against the משנה. Finally, the גמרא asks how the seller can owe an oath over slaves at all. רב says the claim is really about money, and שמואל says it is about a garment or sheaves.

steps.title: A baby born around the time of the sale: they split it
steps.stepSummary: When a cow traded for a donkey, or a sold שפחה, gives birth and each side says the birth happened while the mother belonged to him, they divide the baby's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone traded a cow for a donkey, and the cow gave birth. Or someone sold his maidservant, and she gave birth. The seller says: 'It was born before I sold, so it's mine.' The buyer says: 'It was born after I bought, so it's mine.' They split it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה rules on a case where nobody knows whether a baby was born before or after a sale, and both sides claim it. The answer is that they split it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides make an equally sure claim, and neither one can prove it. Since neither claim is stronger, the משנה does not give the baby to one side. They divide its value.
steps.confusionAlert: You might expect the seller to win because he was the original owner. The גמרא raises exactly this question in Step 8. It explains the split in Steps 7–9: the baby is in no one's domain, and the משנה follows סומכוס, who splits money in doubt.

phrases.english: MISHNA
One who exchanges a cow for a donkey, and it gave birth,
phrases.notes: The cow had a calf, and nobody knows if that happened before or after the trade.

phrases.english: and similarly one who sells his maidservant, and she gave birth,
this one says: before I sold,
and that one says: after I bought
– they divide.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening ruling of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When both buyer and seller each make a sure claim about when the birth happened, they split the value of the baby.

steps.title: Big or small item: the buyer is sure and the seller doesn't know
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sets up a case of two slaves or two fields, one big and one small. If the buyer is sure he bought the big one and the seller doesn't know, the buyer gets the big one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He had two slaves, one big and one small, or two fields, one big and one small, and he sold one of them. The buyer says: 'I bought the big one.' The seller says: 'I don't know.' The buyer gets the big one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה first describes the setup (two items, one big and one small) and then gives the first ruling: a sure buyer against an unsure seller wins the big one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the first case, here only one side is sure. A person who says 'I know' beats a person who says 'I don't know,' so the buyer's sure claim decides it.

keyTerms.meaning: the other one (the other side of the deal)
he is entitled to / he acquires

phrases.english: He had two slaves,
one large and one small,
phrases.notes: 'Large' here means worth more, and 'small' means worth less.

phrases.english: and similarly two fields,
one large and one small.
The buyer says: I bought the large one,
and the other one says: I do not know
phrases.notes: Here 'the other one' is the seller.

phrases.english: – he is entitled to the large one.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ לוֹ שְׁנֵי עֲבָדִים, אֶחָד גָּדוֹל וְאֶחָד קָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case in the משנה. Here only one side is sure, unlike step 1 where both were sure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sure buyer against a seller who doesn't know receives the large item.

steps.title: Big or small item: the seller is sure and the buyer doesn't know
steps.stepSummary: If the seller is sure he sold the small one and the buyer doesn't know, the buyer gets only the small one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The seller says: 'I sold the small one.' The buyer says: 'I don't know.' The buyer gets only the small one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה flips the previous case: now the seller is the sure one, so the buyer gets only the small item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same logic as step 2 now works in the seller's favor. Whoever is sure wins against the one who doesn't know, no matter which side of the sale he is on.

keyTerms.meaning: he has nothing but / he gets only

steps.whatToRemember: Three cases: both sides sure → split (step 1). Buyer sure, seller unsure → buyer gets the big one (step 2). Seller sure, buyer unsure → buyer gets only the small one (step 3). The side that is sure beats the side that doesn't know.

phrases.english: The seller says: I sold the small one,
and the other one says: I do not know
phrases.notes: This time 'the other one' is the buyer.

phrases.english: – he has only the small one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 2, with the roles reversed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sure seller against a buyer who doesn't know means the buyer receives only the small item.

steps.title: Both sides are sure but disagree: the seller swears
steps.stepSummary: If the buyer insists he bought the big one and the seller insists he sold the small one, the seller takes a שבועה and the buyer gets the small one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this one says 'the big one' and that one says 'the small one,' the seller swears that he sold the small one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a third version of the big-and-small case. This time both sides are certain, and each says something different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Steps 2 and 3 only one side was sure, so the sure side won. Here both are sure, so the seller has to back up his claim with a שבועה. After he swears, the buyer takes only the small one.

keyTerms.meaning: The big one / the small one

phrases.english: This one says: the big one
phrases.notes: This is the buyer, claiming he bought the big slave or field.

phrases.english: and that one says: the small one,
the seller swears
that he sold the small one.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה אוֹמֵר גָּדוֹל וְזֶה אוֹמֵר קָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of cases: now both sides are certain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When both are certain and disagree, the seller swears that he sold the small one, and the buyer gets the small one.

steps.title: Neither side knows: they divide
steps.stepSummary: If both buyer and seller say they don't know which one was sold, they divide.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this one says 'I don't know' and that one says 'I don't know,' they divide.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the last version of the case: nobody knows which one was sold. The ruling is that they divide.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one has a sure claim, and no one can swear. So the משנה splits the doubt between the two sides instead of giving everything to one of them.
steps.whatToRemember: The full משנה: if one side is sure and the other doesn't know, the sure side wins. If both are sure, the seller swears. If neither knows, they divide.

phrases.english: This one says: I do not know,
and that one says: I do not know,
they divide.
phrases.notes: They split the difference in value between the big one and the small one.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה אוֹמֵר: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ, וְזֶה אוֹמֵר: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final case of the משנה, where both sides are uncertain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When neither side knows, they divide.

steps.title: Why divide? Whoever holds the baby should keep it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה says they divide the baby's value. We should check who has the baby now and make the other side bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why do they divide? Let us see in whose possession it is standing, and the other one will be 'the one who takes from his friend, and must bring proof'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts discussing the משנה. It challenges the ruling to divide in the first case, the baby born around the time of the sale (Step 1).
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a basic rule called המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה: whoever wants to take something away from the person holding it must bring proof. The baby must be in someone's possession, so that person should keep it unless the other side proves otherwise. So why does the משנה say to divide?

keyTerms.meaning: In the possession or domain of
Whoever wants to take from another must bring proof

steps.confusionAlert: This question is about the FIRST case of the משנה, the baby born to the cow or the שפחה (Step 1). It is not about the 'I don't know' case right before it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that splitting is not the default. Normally the person holding the item keeps it, so dividing needs a special explanation.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Why do they divide?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the baby born to the cow or the שפחה, from the beginning of the משנה.

phrases.english: Let us see in whose possession it is standing,
and the other one will be
the one taking from his fellow, and the proof is on him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה to the גמרא and challenges the ruling in Step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that buyer and seller divide the baby's value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the rule המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, whoever has the baby keeps it, and the other side needs proof. Dividing seems to ignore this rule.

steps.title: The baby is in a place belonging to no one
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין, quoting שמואל, says the calf is standing in a marsh, and the שפחה's child is in an alley. Neither place belongs to the buyer or the seller, so no one holds it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אבין said in the name of שמואל: It is a case where it is standing in a marsh. A שפחה too, where the child is standing in an alley.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the question by setting the case in a place that belongs to neither side. That way the rule about possession does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule המוציא מחבירו only works when one side holds the item. In a marsh or a public alley, neither buyer nor seller holds it. With no one in possession and no proof, they divide. The same answer works for both the cow's calf and the שפחה's child.

keyTerms.meaning: Marsh, a place with no owner
Alley, a side lane that is not anyone's private property

steps.whatToRemember: For the משנה to rule that they divide, the baby must be in a place that belongs to neither side. If one side held it, he would keep it unless the other brought proof. The next step shows this alone is not enough.

phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Avin said
that Shmuel said:
It is where it is standing in a marsh.
phrases.notes: He means the calf. A marsh is not the buyer's land or the seller's land.

phrases.english: A maidservant too,
where it is standing in an alley.
phrases.notes: The child is in a side lane that belongs to neither side.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: בְּעוֹמֶדֶת בַּאֲגַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in Step 6 by narrowing the case of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה deals with a baby located where no one has possession
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed the baby is in the possession of the buyer or the seller, so the holder should keep it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The calf is in a marsh and the child is in an alley, places owned by neither side. With no possession and no proof, they divide.

steps.title: Leave the baby with its original owner
steps.stepSummary: Even if no one holds the baby now, the seller was its first owner, so it should stay with him and the buyer should need proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us leave the baby with its first owner, the seller. Then the other side, the buyer, is the one trying to take money from his fellow, so he must bring proof!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the answer from Step 7. Even if the baby stands in no one's property, the seller owned it first, so it should stay with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 showed that no one physically holds the baby now. The גמרא now points to a different kind of hold: the seller owned the mother, and the baby inside her, before the sale. That gives the seller a חזקה, so the buyer becomes the one taking from his fellow and needs proof. Without proof he should get nothing, not half.

keyTerms.meaning: The presumption that something stays with the person who owned it first
The person who wants to take money from someone else must bring proof

phrases.english: But let us establish it in the presumed ownership of its first owner,
phrases.notes: The first owner is the seller. He surely owned the baby while it was still inside its mother.

phrases.english: and let the other one be
"the one who takes from his fellow, the burden of proof is on him!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that the baby is in no one's domain (Step 7) but raises a further problem: the seller's earlier ownership
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of the משנה that the two sides divide the baby's value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even with no one holding the baby now, the first owner keeps a חזקה. That puts the burden of proof on the buyer, so dividing should not be the outcome.

steps.title: The משנה follows סומכוס
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה follows סומכוס, who rules that money in doubt is split without a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this משנה? It is סומכוס. He says that when money is in doubt, the two sides divide it without taking an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by saying our משנה follows the view of סומכוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most opinions say the one taking from his fellow needs proof. סומכוס disagrees: when it is unclear whose money it is, the two sides simply split it. He does not give the first owner's חזקה the final word, and no one has to swear. That explains why the משנה says they divide.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this? (asked to tie a ruling to a specific תנא)
Money whose owner is in doubt
They split it, and no one takes an oath

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think סומכוס is the standard rule. Most opinions follow המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה. The גמרא is only explaining that this particular משנה follows סומכוס.

phrases.english: Whose view is this? It is Sumakhos,
who says: money that lies in doubt,
they divide it without an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 8 by assigning the משנה to סומכוס
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first owner's חזקה should win, and the buyer would need proof
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה follows סומכוס, who splits money in doubt and does not rely on the first owner's hold

steps.title: Did סומכוס say this when both sides are sure?
steps.stepSummary: Maybe סומכוס only splits when both sides are unsure, but in our משנה both sides claim to be certain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fine, סומכוס said this when each side says "maybe." But did he say it when each side says "I am sure"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave. Maybe the rule of סומכוס only works when both sides admit they don't know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting makes sense when neither side really knows the truth, which is called שמא ושמא. In our משנה, though, each side insists he knows what happened, which is called ברי וברי. So it is not clear that the rule of סומכוס fits our משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Both sides say "maybe": neither one is sure

phrases.english: Say that Sumakhos said this
in a case of "maybe" against "maybe,"
but in a case of "certain" against "certain," did he say it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 9 by questioning whether the rule of סומכוס covers our kind of case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule of סומכוס may only cover cases where both sides are unsure. Our משנה has both sides claiming certainty, so his rule may not apply.

steps.title: סומכוס splits even when both sides are sure
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא says that סומכוס splits the money even when both sides claim to be certain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: Yes, סומכוס said his rule even when each side says "I am sure."
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא answers the question: the rule of סומכוס covers cases where both sides claim to be sure too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This widens the rule of סומכוס. Even when both sides make firm claims, the money is still in doubt from the court's point of view, so they split. That makes our משנה fit סומכוס after all. This is the first of the views the גמרא brings on this point.
steps.whatToRemember: Our משנה follows סומכוס: money in doubt is split without a שבועה. According to רבה בר רב הונא, this is true even when both sides claim to be sure (ברי וברי).

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
Yes, Sumakhos said it
even in a case of "certain" against "certain."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא: אִין, אָמַר סוֹמְכוֹס אֲפִילּוּ בְּבָרִי וּבָרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 10 and saves the attribution to סומכוס
steps.terutzResolutionType: Widening the scope of a תנא's rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: סומכוס splits only when both sides are unsure (שמא ושמא)
steps.terutzMaskana: סומכוס splits even when both sides claim certainty (ברי וברי), so our משנה fits his view

steps.title: רבא: סומכוס only splits when both sides are unsure
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with רבה בר רב הונא. He says סומכוס splits only when both sides are unsure, and he rereads our משנה so that both sides say 'perhaps'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Really, סומכוס only said his rule when both sides say 'perhaps'. He did not say it when both sides claim to be certain. So read the משנה this way: the seller says 'perhaps it was born before I sold it,' and the buyer says 'perhaps it was born after I bought it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer to the question from step 10. Instead of stretching סומכוס's rule, he changes how we read the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 asked how סומכוס could split the money when both sides claim to be sure. רבה בר רב הונא said סומכוס splits even then. רבא says no: סומכוס splits only when both sides are unsure, so the משנה must be read as a case of 'perhaps against perhaps'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Certain.' A claim made with full confidence.
'Really' or 'actually.' It brings back an idea that was being pushed aside.

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not adding a new case. He is saying the words of the משנה should be read as 'perhaps', even though the plain text sounds like both sides are sure.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Really, when Sumakhos said [his rule of splitting],
it was for 'perhaps' against 'perhaps',
but for 'certain' against 'certain' he did not say it.
And teach [the Mishnah this way]:

phrases.aramaic: זֶה אוֹמֵר שֶׁמָּא עַד שֶׁלֹּא מָכַרְתִּי,
phrases.english: This one says: perhaps [it was born] before I sold,
and that one says: perhaps [it was born] after I bought.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לְעוֹלָם כִּי אָמַר סוֹמְכוֹס שֶׁמָּא וְשֶׁמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from רבה בר רב הונא's answer in step 11 to the question in step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה describes both sides claiming to be certain, which seems to go against סומכוס.
steps.terutzMaskana: סומכוס only splits in 'perhaps against perhaps', and the משנה is read as that kind of case.

steps.title: Challenge to רבה בר רב הונא from the end of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The end of the משנה teaches that when both sides say 'I don't know', they split. That fits רבא well. But for רבה בר רב הונא, why would the משנה need to teach the easier case?
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if this one says 'I don't know' and that one says 'I don't know', they split. This fits רבא: the end of the משנה is 'perhaps against perhaps', so the beginning is also 'perhaps against perhaps'. But רבה בר רב הונא said סומכוס splits even when both are certain. If the משנה already said they split when both are certain, why would it need to say they split when both are unsure?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last part of the משנה and uses it to attack רבה בר רב הונא's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, both parts of the משנה are 'perhaps' cases, so nothing is extra. For רבה בר רב הונא, the first part is already the harder 'certain against certain' case. So the later 'perhaps against perhaps' case seems obvious and unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It works well for...' This sets up a contrast with a view that has a problem.
The first part of a משנה.
The last part of a משנה.
'Is it needed?' This asks why something obvious would be taught.

phrases.english: We learned [in the Mishnah]:
This one says: I do not know,
phrases.notes: This is a later case in the same משנה, where neither side knows which item was sold.

phrases.english: and that one says: I do not know. They split.
It works well according to Rava:
since the last part is 'perhaps against perhaps',
the first part is also 'perhaps against perhaps'.
But according to Rabba bar Rav Huna,
who said: Yes, Sumakhos said [to split]
even with 'certain against certain',
now, if with 'certain against certain' he says they split,
is it needed [to teach] 'perhaps against perhaps'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two answers and challenges רבה בר רב הונא's answer from step 11, using רבא's answer from step 12 as the contrast.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר רב הונא's claim that סומכוס splits even when both sides claim to be certain.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the first part of the משנה already rules to split in the harder 'certain' case, then the easier 'perhaps' case in the last part seems unneeded.

steps.title: The end of the משנה shows what the beginning means
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רבה בר רב הונא. The 'perhaps' case at the end was taught so we would understand that the first case is 'certain against certain', and the money is still split.
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is the only problem, it is not a real problem. The משנה taught the last part to explain the first part. Otherwise you might think the first part was only 'perhaps against perhaps', and that 'certain against certain' is not split. So the משנה taught a 'perhaps' case at the end. That tells us the first part must be 'certain against certain', and even so they split.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against רבה בר רב הונא. The extra case at the end of the משנה is there for a purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last case is not a separate, obvious ruling. It is a signal: since the end is clearly a 'perhaps' case, the beginning must be something different, which is 'certain against certain'. So the משנה itself teaches that סומכוס splits even when both sides claim to be sure.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not a problem.' The challenge does not prove anything.
'By implication.' Something we learn because of what was said.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views. רבה בר רב הונא says סומכוס splits even when both sides are certain, and the end of the משנה shows that the first part is a 'certain' case. רבא says סומכוס splits only when both are unsure, and he reads the משנה as 'perhaps' cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common גמרא tool: a later case in a משנה can be there to define what an earlier case was about.

phrases.english: If it is because of this, it is no problem:
he taught the last part to make clear the first part,
so that you should not say the first part is 'perhaps against perhaps',
but with 'certain against certain' [they do] not [split].
[So] he taught the last part as 'perhaps against perhaps',
which shows that the first part is 'certain against certain',
and even so, they split.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מִשּׁוּם הָא – לָא אִירְיָא: תְּנָא סֵיפָא לְגַלּוֹיֵי רֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13 and defends רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that an extra case in the משנה has a purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'perhaps' case at the end of the משנה seems unneeded for רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The end of the משנה was taught to show that the first part is 'certain against certain', and the money is still split.

steps.title: Why does the seller swear instead of splitting?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that when one side says the large slave was sold and the other says the small one, the seller swears. That fits רבא, but for רבה בר רב הונא the משנה should have said they split.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: if one says the large one was sold and the other says the small one, the seller swears that he sold the small one. This fits רבא, who says סומכוס only splits in a case of 'perhaps' against 'perhaps', not 'certain' against 'certain'. That is why there is an oath here. But רבה בר רב הונא says סומכוס splits even in 'certain' against 'certain'. So why does the seller swear? The משנה should have said they split!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another line from the משנה to challenge רבה בר רב הונא. In this case both sides are certain, yet the money is not split.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides make sure claims here, a case of בָּרִי against בָּרִי. רבה בר רב הונא said סומכוס splits even in such a case, so we would expect יחלוקו. Instead the משנה says the seller swears, which fits רבא only.

phrases.english: We learned: This one says 'the large one'
and that one says 'the small one' —
the seller swears that he sold the small one.
It works well according to רבא, who said:
when סומכוס said his rule, it was for 'perhaps' against 'perhaps',
but for 'certain' against 'certain' he did not say it —
that is why he swears.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא דְּאָמַר:
phrases.english: But according to רבה בר רב הונא, who said:

phrases.aramaic: אִין, אָמַר סוֹמְכוֹס אֲפִילּוּ בָּרִי וּבָרִי –
phrases.english: Yes, סומכוס said it even for 'certain' against 'certain' —
why does the seller swear?
It should have said 'they split'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבה בר רב הונא from the end of the משנה, the גמרא challenges him again from a different case in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר רב הונא's claim that סומכוס splits even in 'certain' against 'certain'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the large-or-small slave case both sides are certain. If סומכוס splits there, the משנה should say יחלוקו, not that the seller swears.

steps.title: סומכוס agrees there is no splitting when a Torah oath applies
steps.stepSummary: סומכוס's splitting rule does not apply where a Torah oath is required. This will be explained later.
steps.simpleTranslation: סומכוס agrees that where there is an oath from the Torah, the money is not split, as we will need to explain later on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה בר רב הונא. It says סומכוס himself agrees that a Torah oath settles the case instead of splitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not take back רבה בר רב הונא's view. It adds a limit: splitting applies only when there is no שבועה דאורייתא. Here the seller owes a Torah oath, so he swears and keeps his claim.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath required by the Torah

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a limit on סומכוס's rule. It also leads straight into the next question: why is this a Torah oath at all?

phrases.english: סומכוס agrees that where
there is an oath from the Torah,
as we will need to say later on.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹדֶה סוֹמְכוֹס הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא שְׁבוּעָה דְאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule: סומכוס's splitting does not apply where a Torah oath is required.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought that according to רבה בר רב הונא, סומכוס splits in every 'certain' against 'certain' case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Where a שבועה דאורייתא applies, even סומכוס agrees the oath decides the case and there is no splitting.

steps.title: Why is there an oath when nothing claimed was admitted?
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the case of two slaves, the גמרא asks why the seller swears at all. The buyer claimed the large slave, which the seller denied. The seller admitted the small slave, which the buyer never claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he had two slaves, one large and one small, and so on. Why should the seller swear? What the buyer claimed, the seller did not admit to. And what the seller admitted to, the buyer did not claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question on the same case from the משנה. It asks why there is an oath here at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Torah oath normally comes when the defendant admits part of what was claimed. Here the claim (the large slave) and the admission (the small slave) do not overlap at all. So the reason for an oath seems to be missing, and this also threatens the answer of Step 16.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not why the seller wins. It is why he needs to swear, since he admitted nothing the buyer asked for.

phrases.english: If he had two slaves,
one large and one small (and so on).
phrases.notes: 'And so on' points to the rest of the משנה's case: the buyer says large, the seller says small, and the seller swears.

phrases.english: Why should he swear?
What the buyer claimed from him, he did not admit to him,
and what he admitted to him, the buyer did not claim!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי יִשָּׁבַע? מַה שֶּׁטְּעָנוֹ לֹא הוֹדָה לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 16 rested on the seller owing a Torah oath. Now the גמרא asks why there is any oath in this case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the seller swears in the case of two slaves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath needs an admission to part of the claim. Here the claim and the admission are about different slaves, so there is no basis for an oath.

steps.title: Another problem: the small slave is a case of 'here it is, take it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second reason the seller should not have to swear. He is handing over the small slave right now, so this counts as הילך.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: it is a case of 'here it is, take it'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps building its challenge from Step 17. It adds a second reason why the seller should not need to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath for admitting part of a claim (מודה במקצת) only applies when the person admits he owes something. Here the seller hands the small slave over right away. That counts as הילך, giving it back on the spot, and it is not considered admitting part of the claim. So the oath should fall away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Here it is, take it': handing over the item right away, which is not counted as admitting part of a claim
'And furthermore': adds another problem on top of the last one

phrases.english: And furthermore: it is 'here it is, take it'.
phrases.notes: He means the small slave the seller admits to. He is handing it over right now, not just promising to pay later.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Continuation of the קשיא in Step 17
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second objection to the challenge in Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in the משנה that the seller swears
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Admitting by handing the item over right away (הילך) does not create an oath for admitting part of a claim.

steps.title: Another problem: no oath is taken over slaves
steps.stepSummary: A third problem: by Torah law, nobody takes an oath over claims about slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: one does not swear about slaves!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third problem: claims about slaves never get a Torah oath at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slaves are treated like land, and Torah oaths do not apply to claims about land. They only apply to movable things. So even if the first two problems were solved, an oath over slaves still makes no sense. All three problems together set up the need to find a new way to read the case.

keyTerms.meaning: No oath is taken over claims about slaves, because they are treated like land

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two problems. הילך is about how the seller admitted. This problem is about what the claim is about (slaves), and it would block the oath even without the other problems.

phrases.english: And furthermore: one does not swear
about slaves!
phrases.notes: Slaves are treated like land here, and Torah oaths do not apply to land.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Continuation of the קשיא in Step 17
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third objection to the same challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in the משנה that the seller swears
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Torah oaths are never taken over claims about slaves.

steps.title: רב: the claim is about money paid for the slave or field
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the buyer is really claiming money: the price of a large slave or field. The seller admits only to the price of a small one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: The case is where the buyer claims money. He says he paid the price of a large slave, and the seller admits to the price of a small slave. Or he says he paid the price of a large field, and the seller admits to the price of a small field.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers all three problems at once. He reads the משנה as a fight over money, not over the slave or field themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the claim is about money, all three problems are solved. Money is movable, so the 'no oath over slaves' rule does not apply. The seller does not hand anything over on the spot, so it is not הילך. And the seller is admitting to part of the very same thing the buyer claimed, money, so it is a real case of admitting part of a claim.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Where he claims from him': the case is one where the buyer's claim is...

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common move in the גמרא: to save a ruling, it redefines exactly what is being claimed.

phrases.english: רב said: Where he claims money from him,
the price of a large slave,
the price of a small slave.
the price of a large field,
the price of a small field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the three objections from Steps 17 to 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (the claim is about money)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer and seller are arguing about which slave or field was sold.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are arguing about how much money was paid. Money is movable, so the oath fits.

steps.title: שמואל: the claim is about the slave's clothing or the field's sheaves
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the claim is about movable things that go with the slave or field: a slave's garment, or the sheaves from a field.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The case is where the buyer claims the garment of a large slave, and the seller admits to the garment of a small slave. Or the buyer claims the sheaves of a large field, and the seller admits to the sheaves of a small field.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a different answer from רב. He reads the claim as being about movable items connected to the slave or field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clothing and cut sheaves are movable things, so a Torah oath can apply to them. Both buyer and seller are talking about the same kind of item, and the seller admits to a smaller one. So this is a proper case of admitting part of a claim. Like רב, שמואל solves the problems by changing what is being claimed. He just picks objects instead of money.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רב and שמואל agree the משנה cannot be about the slaves or fields themselves, because no oath is taken over those. רב says the claim is about money. שמואל says it is about movable items (a garment or sheaves).

phrases.english: And שמואל said: Where he claims from him
the garment of a large slave,
the garment of a small slave.
the sheaves of a large field,
phrases.notes: He means grain that has already been cut. That counts as movable, not as part of the land.

phrases.english: the sheaves of a small field.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בְּטוֹעֲנוֹ כְּסוּת עֶבֶד גָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the same objections that רב answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (the claim is about movable items)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The claim is about the slaves or fields themselves.
steps.terutzMaskana: The claim is about the slave's garment or the field's cut sheaves. These are movable, so the oath fits.
